newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH PHONE BID HOAXER POSES AS DUTCH PTT UNIT.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH PHONE BID HOAXER POSES AS DUTCH PTT UNIT.

text.p: A fake bid apparently based on information available on the internet has delayed the privatisation of a Finnish local telephone operator, officials said on Wednesday.

The council of the city of Turku on Monday had to postpone a decision to sell its telephone operator Turun Puhelin after a fax was presented that looked like a bid from Dutch PTT Telecom -- part of Dutch PTT -- but proved later to be an elaborate hoax.

"At first glance, this looks real ... but a second read reveals details that show it is not," said director Aatos Hallipelto at investment banking firm PCA Coporate Finance, the city's adviser on the sale.
The phoney offer upped the real bids on all key points, and was quite skillfully written based on documents "that could easiest be obtained via the Internet," Hallipelto said.
The document, two A4 size sheets, arrived on Monday showing PTT Telecom's fax number as the sender, but that number can easily be manipulated, fax manufacturers say.
According to some media reports, experts believe the fax was sent from Finland since its timestamps suggest it was sent in Finland's timezone, one hour ahead of the Netherlands.

Finnish media on Wednesday quoted PTT Telecom officials as saying they did not even know the Finnish company was for sale and declined any connection with the offer, pointing to spelling mistakes and differences between the document's forged logo and the original.

Although many people involved had immediately mistrusted the authenticity of the surprise bid at the council meeting on Monday, it had created confusion and the decision to sell Turun Puhelin to either of two real bidders was postponed to June 2, Hallipelto said.
Officials now fear similar incidents in the future as ever more information becomes easily available to people via the internet.

"Anything is possible since there seems to be this sort of interest around," city of Turku secretary-general Pertti Waananen told Reuters. "It is quite a problem and I don't know if there can be any solution, apart from improved awareness."
It was unclear on Wednesday whether police would investigate the incident and officials said they did not know the intention of the hoax.

A transport ministry official monitoring telecommunications said the issue was a purely legal one and did not require any action to regulate telecommunications in Finland, where there are more internet host computers per capita than anywhere else.
